Yes. In the supplied association tables, feminizing GAHT-induced protein changes are much more consistent with menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) than with menopause itself.

Using the 2,791 proteins present in both the GAHT and menopause/MHT tables, 212 proteins were FDR-significant for CPA-GAHT and 80 for SPIRO-GAHT. Among these GAHT-significant proteins, the direction of change was usually concordant with MHT: 147/212 (69.3%) for CPA vs MHT<57, 167/212 (78.8%) for CPA vs MHT>=57, 68/80 (85.0%) for SPIRO vs MHT<57, and 66/80 (82.5%) for SPIRO vs MHT>=57. FDR-significant overlap with MHT was also enriched (Fisher odds ratios 3.77 to 6.24).

In contrast, GAHT changes were mostly opposite to the menopause<57 pattern. Only 32/212 CPA-GAHT proteins (15.1%) and 16/80 SPIRO-GAHT proteins (20.0%) changed in the same direction as menopause<57, and CPA showed a negative all-protein rank correlation with menopause<57 (Spearman rho = -0.321). Many of the same proteins were menopause-associated, but they generally moved in the reverse direction.

The sex-hormone association columns support this interpretation: GAHT-significant proteins were more often concordant with female estradiol associations (74.1% for CPA; 67.5% for SPIRO) and discordant with female testosterone associations (30.2% and 27.5% concordant). Thus, the proteomic signature appears estrogen/MHT-like and anti-menopause-like, rather than resembling the protein changes observed during menopause.
